risks: Minimal: the checklist changes the format of an existing handoff. Risks are disturbance for patients, longer handoffs for nurses, and blame if individual sheets are singled out; review results are reported at ward level only.
consent: Patients are told at admission and at the bedside that the ward is testing a new handoff checklist and may ask not to be woken or included in the bedside part; the handoff itself continues as usual care. Staff take part as part of normal work, and no individual performance data leave the ward.
data: Sheet review records bed number, date, shift and missed item categories; no names or record numbers enter the run chart spreadsheet, which is kept on the ward's restricted drive and deleted after the SQUIRE report.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: patients with limited English, hearing loss or cognitive impairment are less able to take part at the bedside. Interpreter phones are used when available, family members may take part with the patient's agreement, and missed items are reported separately for patients who could not take part, so the change does not protect only those who can speak up.
effectiveness: Success means a sustained shift in missed reconciliation items with stable handoff duration and few patients reporting being woken; a failed balancing measure leads to a revised cycle, not to a claim of success.
efficiency: About one hour of review per week and 10 minutes of huddle time; no new staff or software.
costs: Printing of checklists and staff time within normal shifts; no additional budget.
grants: None needed; a hospital QI award could later fund spread to other medical wards.
partnerships: Ward pharmacist (measurement and double review), nurse manager (huddle time), and two patient partners from the hospital's patient experience group (checklist wording and night rules).
rebPath: Screened by the research ethics office as quality improvement not requiring REB review (QIS-2026-118). A later publication follows SQUIRE 2.0 and the journal's QI policy; no additional data collection is planned for publication.
limitations: Single ward, unblinded sheet review, and an outcome measure that is a process step rather than patient harm.
summary: Minimal-risk QI with ward-level reporting, a bedside opt-out, an equity split for patients unable to take part, and a completed QI screening.
